outputs.L1: The invention relates to an electric power generation system comprising: an alternator (1) configured to be coupled to a drive system (7) and to supply an AC voltage to an output bus (10); a reversible AC/DC converter (2), the AC bus (6) of which is connected to the output bus (10) of the alternator (1); an electrical energy-storage element (3) connected to the DC bus (9) of the converter (2); and a controller (4) configured to respond to a transient load-shedding or charging-impact condition by controlling the converter (2). In the event of load-shedding, the converter (2) draws energy from the output bus (10) of the alternator (2) and stores it in the storage element (3). In the event of a charging impact, the converter (2) draws energy from the storage element (3) and injects it into the output bus (10). The converter (2) is further controlled to inject compensation currents for harmonic currents into the AC bus (10) of the alternator (1).
outputs.L2: The invention concerns an electrical power-generation system that includes an alternator (1) coupled to a drive system (7) and configured to deliver an AC voltage to an output bus (10). A bidirectional AC/DC converter (2) has an AC bus (6) connected to the alternator’s output bus (10), while an electrical energy-storage element (3) is coupled to the converter’s DC bus (9). A controller (4) responds to transient load-shedding or charging-impact conditions by operating the converter (2). During load shedding, energy is drawn from the alternator output bus (10) and stored in the storage element (3). During a charging impact, energy is taken from the storage element (3) and supplied to the output bus (10). The controller also operates the converter (2) to inject compensating currents into the alternator’s AC bus (10), thereby offsetting harmonic currents.
outputs.L3:
The system generates electrical power through an alternator coupled to a drive system. The alternator supplies AC voltage to an output bus, which distributes power to the connected loads.

A reversible AC/DC converter links its AC bus to the alternator’s output bus, while an electrical energy-storage element is connected to the converter’s DC bus. This bidirectional arrangement allows energy to flow either from the alternator to the storage element or from the storage element back to the output bus.

During load-shedding events, the controller operates the converter so that excess energy from the alternator’s output bus is transferred to and stored in the energy-storage element. Conversely, during a charging impact or sudden increase in electrical demand, the controller directs stored energy from the storage element into the output bus to support the alternator. At the same time, the converter supplies compensating currents that counteract harmonic currents, thereby helping to maintain the quality and stability of the AC power delivered to the loads.
outputs.L4:
The invention relates to an alternator-based electrical power system capable of maintaining stable power delivery when subjected to rapid load changes and nonlinear loads. The system includes an alternator connected to an AC distribution bus, a reversible AC/DC converter coupled to the bus, an electrical energy-storage element connected to the DC side of the converter, and a controller that regulates bidirectional energy flow through the converter. The energy-storage element may comprise one or more batteries, capacitors, supercapacitors, or another device capable of rapidly absorbing and releasing electrical energy.

The controller monitors operating parameters such as alternator voltage, current, frequency, load demand, and the state of charge of the energy-storage element. Based on these parameters, the controller commands the reversible converter to operate either as a rectifier or as an inverter. This permits the converter to transfer power from the AC bus to the energy-storage element or, when required, from the energy-storage element back to the AC bus.

When a substantial load is suddenly removed, the mechanical input to the alternator may temporarily exceed the electrical power being consumed. Without compensation, this imbalance can produce an increase in alternator speed, bus frequency, or output voltage. In response, the controller operates the converter in a charging mode. Excess electrical energy is drawn from the AC bus, converted to DC power, and stored in the energy-storage element. The converter therefore acts as a controllable temporary load, reducing the effect of the load-shedding transient while retaining energy that might otherwise be dissipated.

Conversely, when a large load is suddenly connected, the alternator may be unable to increase its output instantaneously. The resulting power deficit can cause a temporary reduction in voltage or frequency and can impose a severe torque impact on the prime mover. During such an event, the controller operates the converter in a discharge mode. Stored energy is converted into AC power and supplied to the distribution bus, supplementing the alternator until the alternator and its prime mover can assume the increased load. This action reduces voltage and frequency excursions and improves the dynamic response of the overall power system.

The reversible converter may also provide active harmonic compensation. Nonlinear loads can draw distorted currents containing harmonic components that degrade power quality and increase losses in the alternator and distribution equipment. The controller detects or calculates these harmonic components and commands the converter to inject compensating currents having appropriate magnitudes and phases. The compensating currents substantially cancel the unwanted harmonic currents at the AC bus, causing the current supplied by the alternator to more closely approximate a sinusoidal waveform. The converter may additionally be controlled to provide reactive-power compensation and assist with voltage regulation.

The controller may coordinate transient-energy management and harmonic compensation simultaneously. Priority may be given to maintaining bus stability during major load changes, while the remaining converter capacity is used to reduce harmonics or control reactive power. Charging and discharging limits can be established according to converter ratings, storage temperature, state of charge, alternator operating conditions, and other protection criteria. Once a transient has passed, the controller may gradually restore the energy-storage element to a desired state of charge without introducing another significant disturbance on the AC bus.

By combining bidirectional energy storage with controlled current injection, the system provides both short-term power balancing and continuous power-quality improvement. Excess energy generated during load shedding is captured rather than wasted, while stored energy is made available to support the bus during sudden load application. At the same time, harmonic and, where desired, reactive current compensation reduces distortion and relieves the alternator of currents that do not contribute to useful real-power delivery. The resulting system improves voltage and frequency stability, reduces mechanical and electrical stress, increases usable alternator capacity, and provides cleaner and more reliable power to connected loads.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it points to a specific person, place, object, or idea. Saying “a book” can mean any book, while “the book” refers to one that is already known or clearly identified.

Despite its simplicity, “the” plays an important role in communication. It creates precision, connects ideas, and helps readers understand what a speaker means. It can even add significance: “the answer,” “the moment,” or “the one” sounds more important and certain than a general alternative.

“The” shows that even the shortest words can carry remarkable power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for an electric power generation system using an alternator, a reversible AC/DC converter, an energy-storage element, and a controller that handles load-shedding, sudden charging impacts, and harmonic-current compensation.
counterfactuals.output: An electric power generation system includes an alternator configured to supply an electrical load, an energy-storage element, and a reversible AC/DC converter electrically coupled between the alternator and the energy-storage element. A controller regulates bidirectional power flow through the converter in response to operating conditions of the alternator, the load, and the energy-storage element. During a load-shedding event, the controller causes the converter to transfer excess alternator power to the energy-storage element, thereby limiting alternator overspeed and output-voltage excursions. During application of a sudden charging or other high-impact load, the controller causes stored energy to be supplied through the converter to reduce transient loading of the alternator and stabilize a system bus. The controller further operates the converter to inject compensating current having selected harmonic components that reduce harmonic current drawn from the alternator. The system thereby provides transient-energy buffering, improved voltage and frequency regulation, and harmonic-current compensation using a common converter and energy-storage element.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an aircraft electrical power system in which a reversible AC/DC converter connected between an alternator bus and a storage device smooths transient load changes while also injecting compensating harmonic currents.
counterfactuals.output:
An aircraft electrical power system can use a **bidirectional, reversible AC/DC converter** between an AC alternator bus and an electrical storage device such as a battery or supercapacitor bank.

- **Power generation:** An engine-driven alternator supplies the aircraft AC bus and its connected loads.
- **Energy interface:** The converter operates as a controlled rectifier when transferring energy from the AC bus into storage, and as an inverter when returning stored energy to the bus.
- **Transient smoothing:** A controller monitors bus voltage, frequency, and load current. During a sudden load increase, the converter rapidly discharges the storage device and supplies the power deficit, limiting alternator torque and bus-voltage excursions. During a sudden load decrease, it absorbs the excess power and charges the storage device. The alternator therefore sees a slower, more nearly constant change in demand.
- **Harmonic compensation:** The controller extracts harmonic and reactive components from the measured bus current and commands the converter to inject equal-and-opposite currents. The alternator current consequently remains substantially sinusoidal and at the desired power factor, even when the bus supplies nonlinear loads.
- **Control hierarchy:** Fast inner current-control loops perform harmonic cancellation and transient response, while a slower outer loop regulates storage state of charge and determines the average charging or discharging power.
- **Protection:** Contactors, precharge circuitry, current limiting, isolation, and overvoltage/undervoltage protection disconnect or constrain the converter following faults.

Thus, the same converter functions as both an **energy buffer** for real-power transients and an **active power filter** for harmonic and reactive-current compensation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a concise technical summary of an invention that stabilizes an alternator’s output during load-shedding and load-application transients by bidirectionally transferring energy to and from a DC storage element and providing active harmonic filtering.
counterfactuals.output: The invention stabilizes an alternator-driven AC power system using a bidirectional power converter coupled to a DC energy-storage element. During load shedding, the converter absorbs surplus alternator energy and charges the storage element, limiting voltage and frequency overshoot. During rapid load application, it returns stored energy to the AC bus, reducing voltage sag and frequency droop while the prime mover and excitation system respond. The converter is actively controlled from sensed bus voltages and currents and also injects compensating current to cancel load-generated harmonics, improve waveform quality, and correct reactive-power imbalance. This integrated transient-energy and active-filtering function improves alternator regulation and power quality without requiring substantial mechanical oversizing.
